To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in patients with schizophrenia, slow EEG rhythms are associated with ventricular enlargement, whereas in their relatives they correlate with cognitive deficits.
the power of slow and fast brain rhythms in relatives with genetic risk for schizophrenia is negatively correlated with neuromorphologic characteristics and positively with cognitive indices.
in patients with schizophrenia, the power of slow rhythms of resting EEG is negatively correlated with the sizes of lateral ventricles and with cognitive functions (verbal memory).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of neuromorphologic, psychological and electrophysiological characteristics in patients with schizophrenic disorder and their first-degree relatives.
the search for new markers of schizophrenia risk in the relatives of patients.
the study of the relationship between EEG features, morphological and psychological characteristics in schizophrenic patients and in subjects with a genetic predisposition to schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EEG power changes and neuromorphologic alterations are interrelated in subjects at high risk for schizophrenia, and both are associated with cognitive impairment.

the data presented in this study do not confirm a direct causal relationship between ventricular enlargement and EEG slowing in schizophrenia, and do not support the hypothesis that ventricular dilatation causes EEG slowing in patients with schizophrenia.
EEG is not a reliable indicator of the presence or absence of schizophrenia, and it does not provide a useful means of predicting the onset of this illness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EEG features in schizophrenia are not a direct consequence of ventricular enlargement, but rather are associated with genetic risk factors for the disease.
EEG slowing is a result of a combination of factors, including genetic predisposition to schizophrenia, and is not a direct consequence of ventricular enlargement.
EEG power indices in schizophrenia are not a simple reflection of ventricular enlargement, but they are correlated with neuromorphologic, psychological and cognitive characteristics of the subjects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the study of neuromorphological and psychological correlates of EEG in schizophrenia is of great importance for the development of a new diagnostic approach to schizophrenia and for the development of effective treatment strategies.
the EEG power in the patients with schizophrenia and subjects with familial predispositions to the disease correlates with neuromorphologic features and cognitive parameters.
EEG power indices can serve as markers of genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia and can be used in genetic studies of this disorder.
